features.summary: On a YouTube watch page the Chrome in-page panel offers 'Summarize video', 'Key timestamps' and 'Q&A'. It reads the video's captions from the page, sends up to 30,000 characters to AGI Managed Cloud and answers from them. Videos with no captions say so. Only Chrome has this.

purpose.what_it_does: Reads the captions of the YouTube video in the open tab and uses them as the context for a summary, a list of key moments or questions and answers.
purpose.why_it_exists: Brief item S64.07: the assistant answers questions about a video on the page using its transcript. [inferred] Page text of a video page does not contain the spoken content.
purpose.who_uses_it: Chrome users watching YouTube who want a summary or the key moments.
problems_solved: Watching a long video to find a point.
Page text of a video page being useless for answering content questions.
use_cases: Open a lecture video and press 'Summarize video'.
Press 'Key timestamps' to get a time-marked outline.
Press 'Q&A' for likely questions and answers.

where_to_find_it: Chrome in-page panel on a YouTube watch address (www.youtube.com/watch?v=...): chips 'Summarize video', 'Key timestamps', 'Q&A' (apps/extension/src/features/content/in-page-panel/pageActions.ts YOUTUBE_ACTIONS and isYouTubeWatch; panel chip build apps/extension/src/features/content/in-page-panel/panel.ts:351-368).
prerequisites: Signed in to AGI Managed Cloud (background.ts:9135-9137).
YouTube approved as a site in the extension and the in-page panel left on (apps/extension/src/inPagePanel/setup.ts:70-80 region).
The person opens the panel with the floating launcher button; it does not open by itself (apps/extension/src/features/content/in-page-panel/launcher.ts:1-10).
screens_and_controls: The in-page panel: header with the label 'Managed Cloud · Auto', chips row, text box, response area, disclosure note, 'Open in side panel' link (panel.ts:44-150).
journey: Person opens a watch page and presses the launcher button.
Person presses 'Summarize video' (or another video chip).
The panel shows 'Reading the video captions…' (panel.ts:511).
The captions are read and the answer streams in.
If the person types a free question instead, the panel sends the visible page text, not the captions (panel.ts:558-566).
feedback_and_outputs: 'Reading the video captions…' while loading.
'This video has no captions, so there is no transcript to read. Ask about the page instead.' for none (panel.ts:517-519).
'The video captions could not be read. <reason>' for errors (panel.ts:520).
A disclosure updated to say captions are sent, with the character count (panel.ts:411-430, 523).
settings: In-page panel on or off and site approval in Extension settings.

working: Video id is taken from the 'v' parameter and checked against a pattern (youtubeTranscript.ts:43-51).
Caption data is taken from the page's inline scripts, or fetched from the watch page of the same origin (youtubeTranscript.ts:108-136).

Track choice: a human-written track in the spoken language first, then the default track if human-written, then an auto-generated track, then the default, then the first track (youtubeTranscript.ts:164-178).
Transcript is read as timed text, with the transcript panel as a fallback, and each line is time-stamped like [12:03] (youtubeTranscript.ts:195-210, 257-288, 180-193).
Result status is ok, none or error (youtubeTranscript.ts:1-4, 290-313); the text is cut to 30,000 characters and redacted before sending (panel.ts:522-528).
Each fetch times out after 15 seconds and the page size is capped at 8,000,000 characters (youtubeTranscript.ts:18-19, 119-130).
incomplete: Only the three chips flagged readsVideoCaptions use captions; the free-form text box on a video page sends the visible page text (panel.ts:558-566).
The read depends on YouTube's current page structure and internal endpoints, so it can fail when that changes [inferred] (youtubeTranscript.ts:241-288).
The side panel's 'Add the browser page' on a video page reads page text, not captions; no caption path found there.
not_available: Desktop, Mobile, CLI, VS Code and Web: no transcript reading found.
Other video sites: only the YouTube watch address is recognised (pageActions.ts isYouTubeWatch).

established.statement: The assistant answers questions about a video on the page using its transcript (S64.07).
Page content is untrusted and browser data stays out of global memory by default.

acceptance_criteria: On a watch page, the three video chips appear instead of the generic chips.
A video with captions yields an answer that uses them and the disclosure says 'captions'.
A video with no caption track shows the no-captions message and sends nothing.
When both a human and an auto-generated track exist in the spoken language, the human track is used.
A network failure shows 'The video captions could not be read.' with the reason.
Text over 30,000 characters is cut and the panel says it was cut.
inferred: A free-form question on a video page should also use the captions, since the brief says questions about the video [inferred].
proposed: [proposed] Make the free-form box on a watch page include captions when they exist.
[proposed] Add the same reading to the side panel and to Desktop's paired Chrome.

features.summary: The Chrome side panel is a full chat that stays open next to the page. It keeps its own conversation while the person switches tabs, can add the current page, selected text or tabs as context, and saves its history in the browser. It needs an AGI sign-in. If Chrome lacks the side panel, a popup window is used.

purpose.what_it_does: Provides a persistent chat beside any web page in Chrome, with its own history, new-chat button and temporary-chat mode, and tools for adding page context.
purpose.why_it_exists: Brief item S64.08: a chat sits beside the page in the browser and keeps its own conversation while the person browses. [inferred] A panel lets people ask follow-ups while reading.
purpose.who_uses_it: Chrome users who want to chat while reading or working in tabs.
problems_solved: Switching between a chat tab and the page.
Losing the conversation when moving between pages.
use_cases: Keep a research conversation open while moving through sites.
Ask a follow-up about a different page without losing the thread.
Start a temporary chat that is not saved.

where_to_find_it: Click the AGI toolbar button (title 'AGI Extension') or press Command+Shift+K on Mac or Alt+Shift+K elsewhere (apps/extension/manifest.json:52-72; apps/extension/src/background.ts:7677-7681).
Chrome declares the panel page in the manifest (apps/extension/manifest.json:83-85).
Right-click items also open it (background.ts:7499-7676).
If chrome.sidePanel is unavailable a popup window 440 by 860 holds the same page (apps/extension/src/features/surface/assistantPanel.ts:5-6,12-17,60-70).
prerequisites: Signed in to AGI. The panel has states loading, ready, signed_out and unavailable (apps/extension/src/side_panel.ts:723-726).
screens_and_controls: New chat button (label 'New chat', id sp-new-chat-btn) (side_panel.ts:11533-11545; messages.json:947).
Composer with placeholder 'How can I help you today?' and plus menu items 'Add the browser page', 'Add selected text', 'Attach tabs' (messages.json:212; side_panel.ts:14797-14975).
Model selector, Recents list, temporary chat toggle (side_panel.ts:1095-1100).
journey: Person clicks the toolbar button; Chrome opens the panel for that tab.
If signed out, the panel shows the sign-in state; after sign-in it is ready.
Person chats; replies stream in; history is saved after each turn.
Person switches tabs; the conversation stays and only the page host label refreshes (side_panel.ts:16154-16156).
Person presses New chat to reset the view and start fresh (side_panel.ts:1901-1915).
Person reopens the panel later; the saved conversation is restored (save path side_panel.ts:1294-1331; restore path not opened).
feedback_and_outputs: Streaming answers, thinking indicator, tool activity lines, cards for approvals.
Notices in the composer area for context problems.
When the real side panel is open the in-page launcher hides (apps/extension/src/inPagePanel/setup.ts:8-14, 24-34).
settings: Model and effort selectors; ask-before-acting mode; site approvals and blocked sites; in-page panel toggle (side_panel.ts:6030, 11111, 15535).

working: Side panel opens from the toolbar button and from right-click requests (background.ts:7677-7681; assistantPanel.ts:60-70).
Conversation persists to local extension storage and can sync to the cloud account (side_panel.ts:1294-1346, 1375-1390; apps/extension/src/features/background/conversation-history.ts:1388-1440).
New chat clears messages and pending context (side_panel.ts:1901-1915).
Temporary chat skips saving (side_panel.ts:1095, 1296, 1334).
Tab switching does not reset the chat; it only refreshes the host label (side_panel.ts:16154-16156).
incomplete: History restore, recents list and the cloud mirror rules were only skimmed; details are in unknowns.
disconnected_or_disabled: Sync to the cloud applies only to conversations whose turns all ran in Managed Cloud; others stay in the browser (doc: docs/product/experience-contract.md:296-298).
not_available: Web, Desktop, Mobile, CLI, VS Code: no browser side panel (brief status n/a).

established.statement: A chat sits beside the page in the browser and keeps its own conversation while the user browses (S64.08).
Chrome must include a popup or side panel, connected/native host status, ask/act modes and per-site prompts.
Signed-in Chrome conversations whose turns all ran in Managed Cloud mirror into Cloud Conversation history; unknown, Local or BYOK provenance stays browser-local.
Browser data must not enter global memory or synced chat by default.

acceptance_criteria: The toolbar button opens the panel beside the current page.
The conversation survives switching tabs.
New chat empties the conversation and attached context.
A temporary chat is not saved to history.
Signed out, the panel shows a sign-in state and does not send.
Where the side panel API is missing, a popup window opens the same page.
inferred: Reopening the panel should restore the last conversation [inferred from the save code].
proposed: [proposed] Show which tab the conversation was last about when the person switches tabs.

features.summary: In Chrome, when the person turns on 'Browsing history' in Extension settings, the assistant may search the last days of history for a page they visited before. Each search shows a card with Allow this search or Decline. Only titles and addresses are returned. It is built and tested in Chrome; the brief wrongly says missing.

purpose.why_it_exists: Brief item S64.09: when the user turns it on, the assistant can use browsing history as context. Project requirement: browser history access only by explicit request, no always-allow history (doc: docs/product/requirements.md:1207).
purpose.who_uses_it: Chrome users who say 'find the flight page I saw last week'.
problems_solved: Finding a page seen earlier without remembering the address.
Keeping history private: nothing is read without a per-search yes.
use_cases: Ask 'what was that hotel page I read on Tuesday'.
Ask 'find the docs page I had open yesterday about billing'.

features.summary: The assistant sends a browser to a web address, steps back or forward, and reloads. In the Chrome extension it can also open, switch to and close tabs it created. Desktop, the CLI and VS Code reach the user's paired Chrome through Desktop. The Desktop browser pane is driven by the person, not by the assistant.

purpose.what_it_does: Moves a browser page: open an address, go back or forward one history step, reload, and (Chrome extension only) open, switch to or close a tab owned by the task. Every move is checked against the sites the person or the workspace allows.
purpose.why_it_exists: A browsing task starts by getting to the right page, and a mistaken move can lose unsaved work or land on a site the person never approved. The feature gives the assistant that ability while keeping each move inside site rules and approval rules.
purpose.who_uses_it: People who ask the assistant to do something on a website from the Chrome side panel, from AGI Desktop chat, from the CLI or from the VS Code extension; and people who browse by hand in the Desktop browser pane.
problems_solved: The assistant cannot reach a page without a way to open an address.
A person who goes back or reloads by mistake loses unsaved form data, so these moves have approval rules.
A redirect can land on a blocked site, so every landing page is checked.
use_cases: In Chrome the person says 'open the pricing page of this site'; the assistant calls navigate and confirms the page it landed on.
In Desktop chat the model opens an address in the person's paired Chrome and then reads the page.
A task in Chrome opens a second tab to compare, then closes it after the person approves.
In a Desktop coding session the person types a local preview address into the browser pane and uses Back and Reload.

The assistant can go back, go forward or reload the page it is working on.
The assistant can open a new tab or close one as part of a task.

Browser and computer use treats external content as untrusted, has site permission prompts, allowlists and blocklists, and asks before high-impact actions.

steps.what_happens: Chrome: the side panel starts a run on the signed-in account; the loop sends the goal, page text and tool list to AGI Cloud.
The model returns a navigate, history, reload or tab tool call.
The extension resolves the target (adjacent history entry, tab plan), decides whether to ask, shows an approval card if needed.
The extension moves the tab through the Chrome debugger, waits for the page to settle, reads the real URL and checks it against site policy.
Desktop chat: a cloud turn names device_browser_navigate; the web page calls the desktop 'browser_step' command with the address and optional site rules.

Desktop checks site rules, asks for the browser grant once, optionally shows a 'Check this step' prompt, queues the command to the paired Chrome, which acts and answers; Desktop checks the landing address again.
CLI: the model calls browser_navigate or browser_history; the CLI checks site rules, asks the user, and posts the command to Desktop's loopback bridge using a token file.

features.summary: The assistant works on a website for the person: it reads the page, clicks, types, fills several form fields at once, chains steps toward a goal, and calls tools a site declares (WebMCP) in Chrome. It never submits payment or password fields; the person does that. Chrome, Desktop chat, the CLI and VS Code reach it differently.

purpose.what_it_does: Carries out a goal on a website over several steps: search a site, fill forms, click through, and call structured tools that a page declares instead of clicking.
purpose.why_it_exists: People want the assistant to do web chores, not just read pages. Page text is untrusted and forms hold sensitive data, so each step is verified and sensitive fields are left to the person.
purpose.who_uses_it: Chrome extension users with a browser task; Desktop chat, CLI and VS Code users whose assistant drives their paired Chrome.
problems_solved: Repeating a form or search by hand.
Model claims of success that did not happen: each click and typed field is read back and marked verified or not.
Sending passwords or card numbers through a model.
use_cases: In Chrome: 'Search this store for a 12 inch pan and list the first five prices.'
In the CLI: the model lists the page's controls with browser_find, fills a contact form with browser_fill_form, and tells the person to press submit.
In Chrome on a site that declares WebMCP tools: the model discovers them and calls one after the person approves.
A multi-step goal: sign-in is handed to the person (F064-10), then the assistant continues.

established.statement: The assistant runs a search on a website and reads the results back.
The assistant fills in a web form on the user's behalf.
The user gives a goal and the assistant carries it out over several steps on websites.
The assistant calls tools a website declares (for example WebMCP) instead of clicking through the page.
No sensitive action without user approval; page content is untrusted; high-impact actions confirm.
Prompt injection from browser content must be marked and defended.

acceptance_criteria: In Chrome, clicking a button is followed by a result line with the page URL after the click.
In Chrome, typing into a normal field reports 'Verified that field [n] retained the input.'
Typing into a password field in the paired-browser path returns the protected-field refusal and nothing is typed.
CLI browser_fill_form shows each selector and value in an approval prompt and submits nothing.
A site tool call always shows an approval card, even in Full access mode.
A page containing text that tells the model to ignore the user stops the run with a security warning.
inferred: Search on a site is expected to work through generic typing and clicking; a measure of success should read the results page [inferred].
Desktop chat and Chrome should offer the same set of verbs, since the brief lists the same four items for all apps [inferred].
proposed: [proposed] Add browser_find and a batch fill step to Desktop chat.
[proposed] Add a Chrome batch fill tool so forms need one approval rather than one per field.
[proposed] Record whether a typed or clicked step was verified in the Desktop activity list.

steps.what_happens: Chrome reads the page into a numbered element list and scans it for prompt injection.
The goal, page data and tool list go to AGI Cloud; the model answers with tool calls.
The extension computes the target's signature and decides whether approval is needed; shows a card if so.
The click, type or site tool runs through the Chrome debugger on the page and the result is read back.
A site tool executes in the page and returns page-supplied text, which is treated as unverified.
CLI/Desktop: the command goes through Desktop's loopback bridge to the paired Chrome, which acts under its approved-sites list.
The tool result goes back to the model to decide the next step, until it reports or hits the step cap.

features.summary: Shows the person what a browser task is doing and lets them stop it. In Chrome each tool call and result is logged, the task tab is grouped and outlined, an in-page dock offers Stop and Take over, and the run ends with a reason or a summary. Desktop and the CLI list actions with running, done or failed.

purpose.what_it_does: Makes browser actions visible: a step log, a marked task tab, Stop and Take over buttons, an end-of-run summary and reason, and (Desktop) a recent-activity list.
purpose.why_it_exists: An assistant that clicks in a signed-in browser must be watchable and stoppable. The product requirements ask for clear visible state while AGI controls the browser, logs and a manual takeover path.
purpose.who_uses_it: Anyone running a browser task from Chrome, Desktop, CLI or VS Code.
problems_solved: The person cannot tell what the assistant did.
A runaway task cannot be stopped.
A task that quietly ends leaves the person guessing why.
use_cases: Chrome task: the person watches steps appear, then presses Stop when a step looks wrong.
Desktop dialog: after 'Click' the activity row shows done or 'failed: <error>'.
CLI session: terminal lines 'Open(<url>)' and 'Click(<selector>)' show each action.
A task ends because the site was removed from the approved list; the panel says so.

steps.what_happens: The agent loop emits progress events for each tool call and result.
The background broadcasts AGI_CU_STATE (running, paused, stopped with reason) to the panel and the page overlay.
Stop in the panel sends CANCEL_COMPUTER_USE with the run id; the background cancels that run.
Stop on the page dock sends AGI_CU_USER_INPUT command stop; only accepted from the run's tab and top frame.
Cancelling aborts the in-flight model call to AGI Cloud.
Desktop records an activity entry per command and settles it with ok or failed.
The dialog reads the list through the browser_activity command.

features.summary: When a page needs a sign-in, a CAPTCHA or a password or card, the Chrome assistant hands the page to the person and waits. The person can also press Take over at any time, and Continue hands the page back. A handed-over run ends after fifteen minutes. Only Chrome has this; Desktop, CLI and VS Code have no browser handoff.

purpose.what_it_does: Pauses a Chrome browser task so the person can use the page themselves (sign in, solve a check, enter a password or card), then resumes the same task with the new page state.
purpose.why_it_exists: The assistant must never solve human checks or handle credentials and payments. The handoff keeps those with the person without losing the task.
purpose.who_uses_it: Chrome extension users running a browser task on a site that needs a login or a check.
problems_solved: Sites that block automation with a CAPTCHA.
Credentials and card numbers passing through a model.
A person who wants to step in without ending the whole task.
use_cases: The assistant reaches a sign-in page, calls ask_user_to_take_over, the person signs in, presses Continue, the task goes on.
The person sees the assistant about to do something wrong and presses Take over on the page dock.
The person starts clicking on the page; the assistant stops acting automatically and waits.
A purchase step is reached; the assistant hands over so the person checks the amount and pays.

where_to_find_it: Chrome side panel: buttons 'Take over' (visible while a run is active and not paused) and 'Continue' (visible while paused), banner titled 'Your turn' (apps/extension/src/features/side-panel/computerUsePanel.ts:1220-1240, 1313-1320, 796-805).
Chrome page dock: 'Take over' beside 'Stop' (apps/extension/src/features/content/browserRunOverlay.ts:55).
prerequisites: A running Chrome browser task owned by the current panel and tab.
Not an unattended run: an unattended run reports the step as unfinished instead (apps/extension/src/features/computer-use/agentLoop.ts:1481-1486).

'Continue' button with tooltip 'Hand the page back so AGI continues the task' (computerUsePanel.ts:1230-1234).
Handoff banner text: '<reason> Choose Continue when you are done.' (computerUsePanel.ts:1330-1338).
Dock button shows 'You have the page.' while paused and the pointer and glow are hidden (browserRunOverlay.ts:118-123).
journey: The model calls ask_user_to_take_over with a one-sentence reason, or the person presses Take over, or the person types or clicks on the task tab.
The background creates a takeover, starts a fifteen-minute timer, watches user input on the tab and broadcasts a paused state with the reason (apps/extension/src/background.ts:1053-1085).
The panel shows the banner, switches Take over to Continue and focuses Continue.
The person signs in or solves the check on the page.
The person presses Continue.

The background re-reads the tab URL, re-checks that the site is still approved and consented, commits the new page as the intended page, activates the tab and resumes (apps/extension/src/background.ts:7088-7146).
The model receives 'The user handed the page back...' with a fresh page reading (apps/extension/src/features/computer-use/agentLoop.ts:1488-1496).
feedback_and_outputs: Banner 'Your turn' with the reason and the sentence 'If the page is not handed back within 15 minutes, the task ends.' (apps/extension/_locales/en/messages.json cuTakeoverLimit).

'You have the page.' when the person pressed Take over; 'You started using the page, so AGI stopped acting on it.' when input was detected (messages.json cuTakeoverByUserReason, cuTakeoverByInputReason).
If time runs out: 'The page was not handed back within 15 minutes, so the task ended and AGI let go of the tab. Start the task again to continue.' (computerUsePanel.ts:826).
If handing back fails: 'AGI could not take the page back. Try Continue again, or use Stop.' (computerUsePanel.ts:1355-1358).
settings: none found in the code for the handoff itself; the time limit is a constant (runOwnership.ts:17).

working: Chrome tool ask_user_to_take_over is defined and described for sign-in, CAPTCHA, password and card entry (apps/extension/src/features/computer-use/browserToolDefinitions.ts:49-68).
The agent loop waits for the person: handToUser calls requestTakeover and then re-reads the page (apps/extension/src/features/computer-use/agentLoop.ts:1476-1496).
While taken over, other tool calls are skipped with 'Not done: the user took over the page.' (agentLoop.ts:1553-1565).
The system prompt tells the model never to solve a CAPTCHA or guess a credential and to hand over for purchases (agentLoop.ts:1129-1137).

Manual Take over from the panel and from the page dock, and automatic takeover when the person clicks or types on the task tab more than 750 ms after the last agent action (apps/extension/src/background.ts:1014, 7005-7024, 7088-7102).
Fifteen-minute limit ends the run with the takeover_expired reason (runOwnership.ts:17-18; background.ts:1053-1064).
Resume re-checks site approval and consent and cancels with site_access_withdrawn if they are gone (background.ts:7118-7135).
The brief marks Take over and Return control as 'missing' for Chrome; the code has both, so the brief is out of date.
incomplete: The takeover applies to the run's single task tab; handoff on other task tabs was not found (background.ts uses lease.tabId).

No tests were found that name the takeover flow end to end; 'takeover' appears in computer-use-stop-ui.test.ts, composer-browser-task.test.ts, browser-control-contract.test.ts and background-security-guards.test.ts only by text search [not opened].
disconnected_or_disabled: In unattended runs the handoff is switched off and replaced by 'This step needs a person...' (agentLoop.ts:1481-1486).
not_available: Desktop: computer takeover exists for screen control only (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:2604-2606); the paired-browser path and the pane have no handoff; 'Sign in' in Desktop (browserSignIn.ts) signs the person into AGI itself, not into a site.
Web, Mobile, CLI, VS Code: none found.

established.statement: When a site needs the user to sign in, the assistant pauses, lets them sign in, then continues.
When a site shows a CAPTCHA or human check, the assistant hands it to the user and resumes after.
The user takes over the browser mid-task without ending the assistant's run.
After taking over, the user hands control back and the assistant continues the same task.
Browser and computer use needs a manual takeover path.

acceptance_criteria: On a sign-in page the assistant calls ask_user_to_take_over instead of typing a credential.
While paused the Take over button is hidden and Continue is shown.
The assistant takes no action while the person has the page.
After Continue the next model turn includes a fresh reading of the page.
If nothing is handed back for 15 minutes the run ends with the takeover_expired sentence.
Clicking on the task tab by hand pauses the assistant and shows 'You started using the page'.
If the site was removed from approved sites during the takeover, Continue ends the run instead of resuming.

Handoff on Desktop and CLI would need a visible place for the person to act, which the paired Chrome tab already is [inferred].

[proposed] Make the limit configurable instead of a constant.

features.summary: Before the assistant downloads or uploads a file the person must approve it. steps.what_happens: The model calls download_file or upload_file.
The background decides approval is needed and broadcasts an approve request to the panel; for uploads it binds the request to run, tab, URL and target.
The person presses Allow (and for uploads chooses files).
For uploads, the chosen files are sent to AGI Cloud for inspection through the managed attachments client.
The approved bytes are verified and set into the page's file input through the debugger.
A download starts through Chrome's downloads API after site policy allows both the page and the file address; Chrome writes the file.
The loop waits for completion for a bounded time and reports the state.
Desktop: cloud-chat download goes browser_step, grant check, review prompt, bridge to Chrome.

steps.what_happens: Before any Chrome action or download, the extension loads the admin policy (managed first, then local copy) and the user's allowlist and evaluates the page and target for the capability.
The result is allowed, or denied with a reason: admin-blocked, outside-admin-allowlist, not-allowlisted, admin-unavailable.
A denial raises BrowserSitePermissionRequired (needs approval) or an error with the org wording.
Desktop pane: each main-frame request is checked in the session's request hook; blocked or unknown loads are cancelled and the refused host is reported to the page UI.
Clear browsing data: the web settings page calls browser_pane_clear_data; the main process clears storage and cache of the pane session.
Workspace website rules (from the account) travel with a paired-browser step and are checked in Desktop and again in Chrome.

features.summary: In AGI Desktop (Electron), Settings has a Computer use section with an Any app switch, which defaults to off. Turning it on asks macOS for Accessibility and shows Accessibility and Screen Recording status rows with an Open System Settings button. While off, screen steps are refused. On other systems a reason is shown. The Chrome extension has its own consent.

purpose.what_it_does: It is the front door of computer use on Desktop. One switch (labelled 'Any app') turns on letting the AGI agent see the screen and use mouse and keyboard on this Mac. When on, it shows the two macOS permissions needed (Accessibility and Screen Recording) with their status and a button that opens the right System Settings pane. When off, or when the platform cannot do it, every screen step is refused with a reason the model can relay. (apps/web/features/desktop-host/components/ComputerUseSettings.tsx:171-196; apps/desktop/electron/runtime/computerUseSession.ts:261-267)
purpose.why_it_exists: Controlling a computer is high impact, so it must be an explicit opt-in that is off by default, with the operating-system permissions explained where the user needs them. The product requirements demand site/app permission prompts and clear state while AGI controls the computer. (doc: docs/product/requirements.md section 21.4; apps/desktop/electron/garnishCore.ts:570)
purpose.who_uses_it: A person using AGI Desktop on a Mac who wants the agent to work in apps on screen. A tester checking permissions. An engineer extending the permission rows.
problems_solved: The agent cannot touch the screen until the person turns it on.
The person is told which macOS permission is missing and gets a button to open the right pane instead of a silent failure.
On Windows or Linux the person sees a clear reason instead of a broken switch.
use_cases: A Mac user turns on Any app so the agent can fill a form in a native app.
A user sees 'Not allowed' next to Screen Recording and presses Open System Settings to fix it.
A user on Windows opens the section and reads that mouse and keyboard control is supported on macOS only.
A user who turned the switch off finds the agent refuses the next screen step and explains why.

The section renders only inside the desktop shell and returns nothing in a normal browser (apps/web/features/settings/components/WebSettingsModal.tsx:251; apps/web/features/desktop-host/components/ComputerUseSettings.tsx:159).

Web in a normal browser, CLI: no setup exists (brief S65.01: web missing, cli missing). Mobile and VS Code: not applicable (brief).
prerequisites: AGI Desktop on macOS (computer use returns 'supported on macOS only' elsewhere) (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/computerUseService.ts:226-232).

The input helper binary available: packaged builds ship it; a development run compiles it with the Swift toolchain, otherwise the capability is reported unavailable (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/computerUseService.ts:111-117).

A signed-in AGI account and a cloud chat turn that offers screen tools; the steps come from the cloud model and are carried out on this machine (apps/web/lib/hooks/useChatStream.ts:1886-1899).
screens_and_controls: Heading 'Computer use' with hint 'Let AGI see your screen and use the mouse and keyboard in apps you allow.' (ComputerUseSettings.tsx:34-35).

Under the switch, a note shows the unavailable reason when the platform or a permission blocks it (ComputerUseSettings.tsx:174-176).

Row 'Chrome' with a status note ('Connected', 'Paired, but Chrome is not connected right now', 'not paired', 'Chrome cannot reach this app') and a 'Manage' link (ComputerUseSettings.tsx:37-45,198-212).

When enabled: rows 'Accessibility' and 'Screen Recording' with status text (Allowed, Not allowed, Not asked yet, Blocked by your organization, Not needed on this computer) and an 'Open System Settings' button when the status is Not allowed or Not asked yet (ComputerUseSettings.tsx:228-233; DesktopPermissionsSection.tsx:41-90).
Row 'Refused for now' with 'Ask again' when the person refused computer use at the prompt (ComputerUseSettings.tsx:214-226).
journey: 1. Open Settings, then Computer use in AGI Desktop on a Mac.
2. Read that the switch is off (the saved default is off).
3. Turn on 'Any app'. The app saves the setting and asks macOS for Accessibility if it is not yet trusted (computerUseSession.ts:380-388; systemPermissions.ts listForAccessibility).

4. The Accessibility and Screen Recording rows appear. For any row marked Not allowed or Not asked yet press 'Open System Settings'; for an undecided Screen Recording the app first triggers the macOS capture prompt, otherwise it opens the Privacy pane (systemPermissions.ts openSystemPermission).
5. Return to the app: the page re-reads status on window focus (use-computer-use.ts effect on 'focus').

6. Ask the agent in chat to do something on screen. The first screen step raises a native dialog 'Let the agent use your screen?' with 'Allow for this task' (dispatcher.ts:1950-1966), and later each app asks separately.
7. To turn it off flip the switch: this withdraws the grant, kills the input helper and ends any run (computerUseSession.ts:335-342,387).
feedback_and_outputs: Switch state, unavailable-reason note and per-permission status text in the section.

When a run is active, a floating bar 'AGI is using your computer' with Take over and Stop (ComputerUseControlBar.tsx:22-58), and a native notification 'AGI is using your computer' (computerUseSession.ts:213-218).

established.statement: The user turns computer use on in a guided setup that grants the needed permissions.
The product explains which operating-system permissions computer use needs and how to grant them.
Off refuses steps; unsupported platforms show a reason.
established.source: F065-01 feature definition in the area brief

established.statement: Browser and computer use need site/app permission prompts, clear visible state while AGI controls the computer, and a manual takeover path.
Computer use is advertised only where the Electron implementation supports it.
Prefer typed connectors, then controlled browser automation, then screen-level computer use; no fallback bypasses permissions.

acceptance_criteria: With the setting at its default, the Any app switch is off and a screen step returns the 'turned off' refusal.
Turning the switch on on a Mac without Accessibility triggers the macOS Accessibility prompt and shows the Accessibility row as Not allowed or Not asked yet with an Open System Settings button.
After both macOS permissions are granted both rows read Allowed and the unavailable note disappears.
On a non-macOS system the switch shows the note 'Controlling the mouse and keyboard is supported on macOS only; this device runs <platform>.'
Turning the switch off while a run is active ends the run, shows no active bar and the next screen step is refused.
In a plain browser tab the Computer use section is not rendered.
inferred: A tester should be able to complete setup without leaving the section except to macOS System Settings. [inferred from the Open System Settings button]
The refusal text is written for the model so that it tells the user where to switch computer use on. [inferred from computerUseSession.ts:53]
proposed: [proposed] Turn the rows into a guided checklist with a single 'Check again' that detects when Screen Recording needs relaunch.
[proposed] Offer a Windows implementation or hide the section entirely on unsupported systems instead of showing a disabled switch.

steps.what_happens: Person flips Any app in the Settings page, which runs inside the Electron window and calls the desktop runtime command computer_use_set_enabled.
The shell saves computerUseEnabled and, when turning on, asks macOS for Accessibility if it is not trusted; turning off withdraws the grant, stops the helper and ends any run.
The page reads status: support, available reason, grant state, phase and the two system permission states.
Before each chat request the page reads a device declaration; screen capability is declared only if enabled, available and not refused. The declaration is sent as a header to our server.
The server believes the declaration only for desktop and mobile surfaces, removes computer.use if the workspace administrator turned it off, and adds device tools to the model's tool list.
When a step comes back, it runs on the desktop. If computer use is off, a step is refused before any prompt.

features.summary: Everything else in computer use after setup. On Desktop the agent screenshots, clicks, types, scrolls, drags and opens apps, one app at a time with prompts, Refused apps, clipboard and sensitive-step review, loop guard, Escape stop, pause when the user moves the mouse, and hand back. The Chrome extension drives tabs. Web can send tasks to your computer.

purpose.what_it_does: Covers the running experience of computer use: what the agent does on screen, how the person sees and controls it, and where it stops. Desktop (macOS) captures a chosen display, clicks, types, scrolls, drags, presses keys and opens installed apps through a small signed helper, with approval per app, per task and per sensitive step. The Chrome extension drives browser tabs with its own loop, overlay and approvals. The web 'Your computer' page and mobile send tasks to a paired computer. (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/computerUseService.ts header; apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:2555-2613; apps/web/features/remote-dispatch/components/RemoteComputerPage.tsx:1-60)
purpose.why_it_exists: An agent that controls a computer must stay visible, interruptible and bounded. The requirements ask for app permission prompts, allow and block lists, high-impact confirmations, clear visible state, an audit trail and a manual takeover path. (doc: docs/product/requirements.md section 21.4)
purpose.who_uses_it: People letting the agent do tasks in apps or browser tabs; people sending tasks to their own computer from the web or phone; testers and engineers of the Desktop runtime and the Chrome extension.
problems_solved: The agent cannot touch an app the person did not allow or refused.
The person can stop, pause or take over at any moment.
Sensitive steps (payments, passwords, sending) are reviewed before they run.
A stuck agent that repeats itself is stopped.
An offline computer is reported rather than silently ignored.
use_cases: The agent opens a native app, clicks through a form and types, asking once per app.
The person moves the mouse mid-run, the agent pauses, and the person later presses Hand back.
The agent reaches a payment page and a 'Check this step' dialog asks Deny or Allow once.
From the web 'Your computer' page the person sends a task to a paired desktop.

journey: 1. The person asks the agent for a task needing the screen.
2. First screen step: the app asks 'Let the agent use your screen?' (once per task).
3. The agent takes a screenshot of a display; the model sees the picture and which app and window is in front.
4. Before a click or key, the app under the target is asked about: allow once, always or Never allow.
5. Sensitive steps raise 'Check this step'; clipboard keys raise a clipboard question.
6. The step runs. A macOS notification 'AGI is using your computer' appears with the stop key; the bar shows Take over and Stop.
7. If the person moves the mouse or types, the run pauses ('Paused. You have the screen.'). They press Hand back, confirm, and the agent takes a fresh screenshot and carries on.
8. The run ends by Stop, by 2 minutes without steps, or when the window closes; a notification says 'AGI finished using your computer'.

established.statement: The user lists which applications the agent may control.
The user lists applications the agent must never control.
The agent can be pointed at one window rather than the whole screen.
On a multi-monitor setup computer use can target a chosen display.
The user sees what the agent sees on screen as it works.
The agent's pointer position or action target is shown visually as it acts.
The product shows which application and which window the agent is currently working in.
Clipboard access by the agent needs its own permission.
The user grants the agent specific local folders and can revoke them.
The agent can open an application; click and type; scroll; drag and drop.
The agent can work native open/save file dialogs.
The agent can operate an application in the background without taking over the user's screen.
When the user moves the mouse or types, the agent yields rather than fighting for control.
One immediate control stops all computer control.
The user pauses the agent and takes control, then hands control back and the agent continues.
Sensitive actions (payments, passwords, sending) require the user's review before the agent does them.
When sign-in is required the agent hands off to the user and continues afterwards.
Each action leaves a record of what was done and whether it worked.
When an application cannot be controlled the product says why.
When the target computer is offline the product says so and waits or stops clearly.
When a permission is revoked the agent stops and the user is told how to restore it.
From another device the user directs work on their own permitted computer.
Required controls: site/app permission prompts, allowlists and blocklists, high-impact confirmations, no sensitive action without approval, visible state, logs and audit trail, manual takeover.
Never use provider-native tools in Local mode; ask consent before sending computer-use screenshots to the provider.

acceptance_criteria: A click aimed at an app that has no answer raises a per-app prompt naming that app; Never allow adds it to Refused apps and later steps on it are refused without a prompt.
A click or type step landing on AGI Desktop's own window is refused with the own-window message.
Pressing Escape during a run stops it, the helper is killed, the computer.use grant is withdrawn and the next screen step is refused.

Moving the mouse during an active run pauses it within about a second and a notification 'AGI paused' appears; Hand back with Keep control leaves it paused and Hand back resumes it with a fresh screenshot.
A step with a review sentence shows 'Check this step' and does nothing when Deny is chosen.
Pasting with the keyboard asks for clipboard permission once; refusing returns the clipboard-refused message.
Sending the same click five times with no screen change stops with a loop message.
With the paired computer offline, a cloud run reports 'Waiting for <device> to come online' and continues without the device after the wait budget.

steps.what_happens: The cloud model emits a device step request in the chat stream; the page reads it.
The desktop page runs executeDeviceStep, which sends a runtime command with the task run id to the Electron main process. A step for a different device is answered with 'waiting on <device>'.
Main process gate: refuse if off or stopped; ask for computer.use if undecided; confirm the task run; execute.
guardScreenStep starts or resumes a run, handles pause waiting, and applies the loop detector.
For input steps: gate apps, review sensitive step, gate clipboard keys, recheck apps, then run the helper command with the input watch suspended.
The macOS helper posts mouse or key events; screenshots are captured by Electron desktopCapturer and scaled to at most 1280 pixels wide, PNG or JPEG.
Results and any screenshot are posted back to our resume endpoint, and the model decides the next step.
Before a device-bound run continues, the server re-checks the device registry and waits or withdraws device tools.
Chrome: the extension agent loop calls AGI Cloud chat completions, runs browser tools through the Chrome DevTools Protocol in the tab, and shows approval cards.

execution_and_data_flow.models_and_providers: A cloud model chooses each step on our servers; the Desktop returns screenshots to it, so images go to the provider that serves the turn. Default routing for kind 'computer-use' prefers premium computer-use slots, then computer-use, then workhorse slots (packages/contracts/types/src/model-catalog.ts:2879-2889). The extension also sends its run through the same chat completions route. No local-model path was found.

access_and_usage.account: Signed-in AGI account for cloud chat turns, device registry and remote dispatch (useChatStream.ts:1930-1938; agentLoop.ts:120-129).
access_and_usage.permissions: macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording; computer.use; per-task allow; application.control per app; clipboard.read; folder permissions are separate (dispatcher.ts:1099-1108; applicationControl.ts:104-118; computerUseSteps.ts:64-73).
access_and_usage.subscription: Computer-use model slots are listed for Pro, Max and Enterprise and not for Free (model-catalog.ts:1235-1372). The upgrade card for 'computer use' exists (paywall-vocabulary.ts:30-33; InlinePaywallCard.tsx:135).
access_and_usage.limits_and_metering: Unit computer_use_requests counted monthly from managed_usage_requests where quotaFeature is computer_use; soft and hard caps per plan (tier-unit-quota-service.ts:61-65,122-130,175-180; request-processor.ts:6132-6146). Message code computer_use_monthly_limit_reached. The Usage settings page lists the unit (account-usage-client.ts:5-17).
access_and_usage.flags: Workspace feature access computer_use can switch it off for an organization (request-processor.ts:3363-3375). Chrome extension mode ask, auto, full, yolo.
access_and_usage.model_compatibility: Not established; the tool list is the same for any model that serves the turn. Metering follows the model slot [inferred].
access_and_usage.provider_restrictions: none found in the code
access_and_usage.local_mode: Not found. Steps are produced by the cloud tool loop; the Desktop device profile reports localModels false and no local-model driver of computer use was found. The requirement is that Local mode never uses provider-native tools (doc: docs/product/requirements.md:133). How Local mode treats computer use is unknown.

features.summary: Before a coding session starts, the person chooses where it runs: a local folder on the computer, a git worktree (a separate checkout so parallel sessions never touch the same files), or a managed cloud sandbox with a GitHub repository and branch. Each app offers a different part of this choice.

purpose.what_it_does: Lets the person pick the folder or GitHub repository, the branch, the isolation (this folder or a new worktree) and the place (local or cloud) for a coding session before it starts.
purpose.why_it_exists: An agent edits real files. The person must see which files it will touch, and parallel sessions must not overwrite each other. The brief states this as S66.01 to S66.04 (doc: knowledge-base/data/area-briefs/066-coding-workspace-frontend.md). The product contract lists workspace, repository and worktree selection as a developer-screen duty (doc: docs/product/experience-contract.md:262-266).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers using the Desktop app, web /code, the CLI, VS Code, and (behind a switched-off flag) the phone.
problems_solved: Agent edits land in the wrong folder or branch.
Two sessions edit the same working copy.
A person cannot tell whether work runs on their machine or on our servers.
use_cases: On Desktop, choose a repo folder and start a session in 'New worktree' so the working copy stays untouched.
On web /code, pick a GitHub repository and branch and run the task in a cloud sandbox.
In a terminal, run 'agi -w feature-x' to work on a separate branch checkout.
In VS Code, with several folders open, answer the quick-pick to say which folder the operation uses.

established.statement: The user chooses which repository or folder a coding session works on before it starts.
The user chooses the git branch a session starts from or works on.
The user picks or creates a worktree so parallel work stays isolated.
Before starting, the user chooses whether the session runs locally or in a cloud sandbox.
Workspace, repository and worktree selection is a required developer-screen function.
A worktree flag in the app-server stays false until the Rust owner implements and verifies it; the host now reports checkpoints and worktrees true.
Managed Code sessions are capped by the plan's maximum active sandboxes and need a plan that includes AGI Code.

acceptance_criteria: On Desktop with a folder approved, the composer shows the folder name and branch, and the 'Run the session in' radio lists exactly 'This folder', 'New worktree', 'New worktree with my changes' when the CLI reports worktrees.
Starting a session with 'New worktree' leaves the original folder's files unchanged while the agent edits the worktree.
In a browser tab (no desktop host) no Local folders appear and the Cloud choice shows a not-enabled or plan notice when the deployment or plan does not allow it.
A cloud start over the plan's active-session limit is refused with a message that names the limit.
'agi -w' without a name creates a worktree with a made-up name and, if nothing changed, removes it at exit.
In VS Code with two folders open and no active editor, the quick-pick appears; with one folder it does not.
If a start fails, the composer shows a message and the folder's session list gains no new row.
inferred: [inferred] A failed start leaves no half-started session in the UI, because startSession returns null and only refreshes the list on success (use-local-sessions.ts:395-415); whether the CLI removes a half-made worktree is unknown (a cleanupFailures list exists, use-local-sessions.ts:396-399).
[inferred] The 'Local' mode on Desktop is independent of payment: a folder session can run on a local model, while account models need the developer-surfaces plan capability (local-code.ts:700-760).
proposed: [proposed] Add a branch picker and a worktree picker to the CLI and VS Code that mirror the Desktop radio and local branch popover.
[proposed] Show on mobile a read-only note that starting a local session needs the Desktop, instead of a hidden screen.

steps.what_happens: Person picks folder and placement in the composer; state lives in the page draft.
The web app (inside the Electron window) asks the desktop host for folders and branches over the host bridge.
On send, startSession picks a starting model by plan, then calls developer_session_start with environment local or worktree.
The Electron main process starts the AGI CLI agent in the folder or a new worktree; the CLI creates the git worktree.
Cloud path: the page lists GitHub repositories and branches through our API, using the user's GitHub app installation.
Cloud path: POST /api/code/sessions checks plan, active-session count and idempotency, then inserts a cloud_code_sessions row in state provisioning and the sandbox is provisioned.

execution_and_data_flow.models_and_providers: Choosing a place does not choose a model. A Desktop local session starts with a model chosen from the folder's model list and the plan: models installed on the machine are listed as ready; the account's models need the plan capability developer_surfaces (local-code.ts:700-760; use-local-sessions.ts:376-390). Cloud sessions choose a coding harness or image in 'Edit environment' (CodeComposer.tsx:321-376). No provider name is hardcoded in the picker.

access_and_usage.account: Cloud sessions and branch listing require a signed-in account (getUserScopedDb in apps/web/app/api/code/sessions/route.ts:42,69). Whether Desktop local sessions need sign-in is unknown; the host reports managedSignedIn per folder (packages/contracts/local-runtime/src/developer-sessions.ts:355).
access_and_usage.permissions: Desktop asks per folder for shell and git permissions: shell.execute for session start, git.read to list branches, git.write to switch branch (dispatcher.ts:699-925). VS Code worktree removal needs a modal confirmation (sessionWorktrees.ts:25-45). The CLI refuses a worktree through a symbolic link (worktree.rs:226-237).
access_and_usage.subscription: Cloud sessions need a plan with sandboxes and a daily coding budget (planIncludesAgiCode, billing-catalog.ts:839-841). The plan ladder in code is basic, pro, max, max_15x (billing-catalog.ts:32-37); team is a self-serve paid tier. Which plan first includes AGI Code is computed by agiCodeMinimumPlan (billing-catalog.ts:843-845); exact values not listed here. Local sessions on account models need the 'developer_surfaces' capability.
access_and_usage.limits_and_metering: Active cloud sessions are capped by getPlanMaxSandboxes (billing-catalog.ts:801-806) and counted in states provisioning, ready, running (cloud-code-session-service.ts:1250-1256). Metering of sandbox compute exists (compute-metering.ts is cited by the brief; not read). Local worktrees: none found in the code.

features.summary: Shows the person's coding sessions grouped by folder, lets them open one, rename, pin, archive or restore it, and marks each as running, needing approval, waiting for an answer, or failed. On Desktop and web the marks follow live runtime events; the CLI and VS Code have their own pickers and trees.

purpose.what_it_does: Lists coding sessions with readable titles and status marks, and offers open, rename, pin, archive and restore actions.
purpose.why_it_exists: People run several sessions at once and need to find one, know which needs them, and tidy the rest (S66.05 to S66.07, doc: knowledge-base/data/area-briefs/066-coding-workspace-frontend.md).

features.summary: Browse the session folder's files, find a file by name, open several files in tabs and edit them (Desktop and web in Electron), attach files to a message, send a selection to the agent (CLI, VS Code), and explain editor errors (VS Code). The brief's 'missing' for tree and tabs is out of date.

In VS Code run 'Code: Explain Error' on a red squiggle.

2. Expand folders or type a name; results show up to 200 files.

features.summary: Run shell commands tied to the session folder and review what ran. Desktop and web in Electron offer terminal tabs (a real shell, or a one-command-at-a-time fallback) and a list of running commands to stop. Cloud sessions show output, errors and exit codes. The CLI uses a ! prefix and /tasks.

purpose.what_it_does: Gives a terminal attached to the session folder, shows each command's output and exit status, and lists long-running commands so they can be stopped.
purpose.why_it_exists: A coding agent runs commands, and the person needs to run their own and see what ran (S66.15 to S66.17).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers on Desktop, web cloud sessions, CLI, VS Code.
problems_solved: Switching to another terminal app.
Not knowing a dev server is still running.
Not seeing why a command failed.

features.summary: Shows what the agent changed. On Desktop and web in Electron, a Changes panel lists changed files against the last commit with discard, and a Review pane shows each turn's hunks with Stage, Revert and line comments sent back to the agent. The CLI has /diff-review and VS Code has accept and reject diffs.

purpose.what_it_does: Shows line-level diffs and a summary of created, modified and deleted files, lets the person keep or undo single hunks, and send comments on lines back to the agent.
purpose.why_it_exists: People must be able to check and steer what an agent did before it counts (S66.18 to S66.21; doc: docs/product/experience-contract.md:271).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers on Desktop, web (Electron and cloud), CLI, VS Code; mobile for read-only review when enabled.
problems_solved: Trusting changes without seeing them.
All-or-nothing undo.
Explaining a fix request in words instead of on the line.
use_cases: Open Changes after a turn and read the diff of one file.
Review a turn's hunks; stage the good ones and revert the rest.
Write a comment on a line and send all comments back to the agent.
In the CLI run /diff-review and press y or n per hunk.

features.summary: Each prompt or turn saves a point the person can go back to. On Desktop (web UI in Electron) the Review pane rewinds code, conversation or both after a preview. The CLI has /rewind and a Rewind picker. VS Code has a Checkpoints quick-pick. Web in a browser tab and mobile have none.

purpose.what_it_does: Saves the code state and conversation position before each prompt or turn and lets the person restore code, conversation or both, after confirming what will change.
purpose.why_it_exists: Agents sometimes go the wrong way. Going back to a known point is safer than manual undo (S66.22, S66.23; doc: docs/product/experience-contract.md:274).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers on Desktop, CLI and VS Code.
problems_solved: An agent turn broke the project.
Wanting to retry a prompt from the same starting point.
Fear of letting the agent edit.
use_cases: Rewind to before the last turn after a bad refactor.
Restore only the conversation to retry with a different prompt.
In the CLI run /rewind list then /rewind 2 code.
In VS Code pick a checkpoint and choose 'fork and code'.

features.summary: Sets how much the coding agent may do without asking. Cloud sessions on web and desktop use three account-wide policies (ask every time, auto-approve read-only, skip approvals) plus a per-turn Plan mode. Local sessions use Plan, Ask, Auto and Bypass. CLI and VS Code have their own mode pickers. Mobile only edits the account policy in chat.

purpose.what_it_does: Lets the person choose whether the agent may read, edit files and run commands on its own, or must wait for a yes. Plan mode lets the agent read and propose changes while it cannot edit. When the agent does ask, the person answers in the same surface. The running session enforces the choice: in cloud, the server decides per tool call (apps/web/lib/services/cloud-code-agent-tools.ts:345-380); in local sessions the AGI CLI enforces the mode (apps/cli/src/agent/chat.rs:2355-2365).
purpose.why_it_exists: A coding agent can delete files and run commands, so people need a safe default and a clear way to give it more freedom. The project says an action a user cannot undo asks first (doc: AGENTS.md section 9) and security behaviour fails closed (doc: AGENTS.md section 6).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers who start or watch coding sessions in the web Code page, the desktop app, the CLI and the VS Code extension. Workspace admins also matter, because they can forbid the skip-approvals policy (packages/contracts/types/src/tool-approval-policy.ts, key allowAutonomousToolApprovals).
problems_solved: Stops the agent from changing files or running commands the person did not expect.
Lets a person who trusts the agent skip repeated prompts.
Lets the person review a proposed plan before any edit is made.
Lets an organisation block unattended autonomy for its members.
use_cases: Start a cloud session in Plan mode, read the plan, then switch the mode menu to an editing policy and ask it to apply the plan.
Keep Ask on while the agent works in an unfamiliar repo, approving each edit from the approval card.
On the desktop, run a local session in Auto so edits apply without prompts while commands still ask.
In the CLI, start with the plan permission mode so no mutating tool runs before the plan is approved.

journey: 1. Open the Code page and pick an environment (cloud or local).
2. Open the mode control: 'Approval mode' for cloud, 'Agent mode' for local.
3. Choose a policy or Plan (click, or press the digit shown on the row).
4. Send a task. The agent runs under that mode.
5. When the agent needs permission an approval card appears with the command or edit and the reason.
6. Answer: cloud approve or reject; local allow once, for the session, always allow a command prefix, deny, or deny and stop.
7. The turn continues, or stops if the person chose 'Deny and stop'.

established.statement: The default policy is ask every time.
The account-level cloud default is autonomous (skip approvals) when nothing is stored.
The user can switch the agent into a plan mode where it proposes a plan and makes no edits until approved.
The user chooses a mode where the agent edits and runs tools on its own versus asking first.
The user sets how much the agent must ask (ask every time, auto-approve safe, autonomous) and the running session honours it.
An action a user cannot undo asks first and fails closed.
The menu supports keyboard digit selection.

acceptance_criteria: Cloud web: with no saved policy the 'Approval mode' control shows 'Skip'; choosing 'Ask before every action' persists it and survives a reload.
Cloud web: in Plan mode no file-edit tool is offered to the model and an edit attempt is refused with the plan-mode text.
Cloud web: with 'Ask before every action' even a read-only tool call produces an approval request.
Cloud web: when the workspace forbids autonomy, a stored 'Skip approvals' behaves as ask-every-time on the server.
Local session: choosing Bypass requires a confirmation at the computer; the Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+M shortcut never lands on Bypass.
Local approval card offers 'Always allow' only when a command prefix is proposed; 'Deny and stop' ends the turn.
CLI: in plan permission mode a mutating tool call is refused with 'plan_mode_unapproved' until the plan is approved.
Keyboard: with the cloud menu open, pressing the digit on a row selects it and closes the menu.
inferred: The local and cloud modes are two different systems with different wording; a single wording per surface would reduce confusion [inferred].
Mobile in Local mode keeps its own stored policy in the settings store rather than the account namespace [inferred from toolApprovalPolicyOwner.ts:123-147].
proposed: [proposed] Add an explicit 'Approve plan and start editing' action to cloud Plan mode so it matches the CLI and the brief.
[proposed] Show the active mode inside the mobile code-session view.
[proposed] Offer a per-session policy override in addition to the account default.

steps.what_happens: Cloud: the composer reads the saved default policy from the account preference store when it mounts; on failure it shows the safe default.
Cloud: picking a policy saves it to the account preferences and rolls back the label if the save fails; picking Plan only changes the turn mode in page state.
Cloud: at the start of each agent turn the server reads the stored policy and the workspace rule, and reads the turn mode.
Cloud: for each tool call the loop asks the gate; the result is run, ask (turn stops as awaiting_approval) or refuse.
Cloud: the person approves or rejects through the approvals endpoint and the turn resumes.
Local: the page asks the desktop host to start a turn with the chosen agent mode; Bypass is confirmed by the person in the desktop main process first.
Local: the AGI CLI runs the turn, maps the mode to its permission mode, and emits approval-requested events that the page shows as a card.
Local: the answer goes back through developer_approval_answer; 'always allow' or sensitive decisions are confirmed in the desktop main process.
Phone: a paired phone can answer a desktop approval over the remote link.

features.summary: Shows how much plan usage and how much of the model's context window a coding session has used. Web and desktop show a ring beside the composer with a popover and a warning banner. The CLI shows a context meter and token counts. VS Code shows a status-bar token and credit counter. Mobile shows plan usage and, for cloud tasks, context.

purpose.what_it_does: Gives the person a quick read on two limits: the plan's usage limits (five-hour, weekly) and how full the model's context window is for the session. On the web ring, the arc shows plan usage, and the popover adds a context bar when both numbers are known (apps/web/features/code/components/CodeComposer.tsx:1521-1650).
purpose.why_it_exists: A coding session can run long. People need warning before a limit stops them or the context is full. For Free accounts the product shows only an Upgrade prompt, never meters (doc: owner product decision recorded in project memory 'Free usage = Upgrade only'; code: CodeComposer.tsx:1611-1618; test apps/web/features/code/components/CodeUsageRing.test.tsx:64).
purpose.who_uses_it: Anyone running coding sessions who is on a metered paid plan or wants to see context fill.
problems_solved: Surprise rate-limit stops.
Sessions that silently slow down as the context fills.
Not knowing when limits reset.
use_cases: See the weekly bar at 90 percent and a warning banner with the reset time.
Open the ring popover to check 'Context window' fill during a long local session.
On a Free plan, open the ring and tap Upgrade.
In the CLI, watch the 'ctx' meter go from green to red.

Free plan: the popover shows only 'Upgrade' and no percentage.

proposed: [proposed] Show a money or credit figure next to the percentage for plans that meter by credits.

steps.what_happens: The ring hook fetches the usage summary from the web API with the signed-in cookie and shares it across components.
The server builds the summary from the account's usage records for the user.
The hook revalidates every 300 seconds while the page is active.
Local: after each turn the CLI computes context tokens and sends them in the turn event; the page stores the number.
Cloud: the server adds each turn's token totals to the session row and the page reads them with the session.
The page divides tokens by the model's context window from the model catalog and draws the bar.
VS Code settles billed credits by asking the server for each request's cost.

features.summary: Shows work running beside the main agent. The desktop-hosted web session panel lists subagents (child tasks) with their state and lists commands running in the folder, such as dev servers, with a Stop button. The CLI has a /tasks command. VS Code can list and stop subagents. Mobile has none.

purpose.what_it_does: Shows each subagent the session started, with its title and state, and shows long-running commands in the open folder with how long they have run. The person can stop one command or all of them. A server with a printed address gets a 'Preview' button.

purpose.who_uses_it: Developers running local coding sessions on the desktop, and terminal users of the CLI.
problems_solved: Forgotten dev servers that keep a port busy.
Not knowing what a subagent is doing or whether it failed.
Interrupted work that would otherwise vanish.
use_cases: See 'Subagents (3) · 2 running · 1 done' and open it for titles and states.
Press the stop button next to 'npm run dev' when the session ends.
Use 'Stop all' when several commands run.
In the CLI, run /tasks and then /tasks stop <id>.

features.summary: On the desktop app, the Code session can open a built-in browser pane that shows the page the agent is building, and, on a Mac, a live iOS Simulator pane that can be docked or floated. A running dev server's printed address gets a Preview button, and errors from the preview page can be sent to the agent.

features.summary: Cloud coding sessions can be shared by link: a team link in a workspace, or a signed-in link for a personal session. Local sessions are not shareable. A local session can be continued in the terminal with a copyable resume command, in VS Code, or from a paired phone that attaches over remote control.

purpose.what_it_does: Share: sets who can open a cloud session (private, team or public-to-signed-in) and gives a link to a read-only view. Continue: gives a way to carry a session to another client: a resume command and VS Code link on the desktop-hosted page, VS Code and CLI continue commands, and phone attach through Remote Control.
purpose.why_it_exists: People want to show a session to a teammate and to move work between machines. The founder decision follows the leaders: only cloud sessions are shared, and cloud results come to a local checkout through the CLI and VS Code (doc: docs/decisions/2026-09-27-founder-decisions.md:334-351).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers and their teammates; phone users watching a desktop session.
problems_solved: Asking a teammate for a screenshot of a session.
Switching from desktop to terminal or editor without losing history.
Approving a desktop agent's request from a phone.

features.summary: A person asks a coding agent about a project folder: where something lives, who calls it, how a request flows. The agent reads files with its read, search and list tools and answers. It runs on Desktop and CLI, in VS Code and, as a phone view, on Mobile. A Web browser tab can only use the cloud sandbox.

purpose.what_it_does: Lets a person ask free-form questions about a code repository. The coding agent answers by reading the repository's files rather than guessing. It covers structure overviews, finding where a thing is defined, finding where a symbol is used, and tracing a call from entry point to effect.
purpose.why_it_exists: The first step of almost every coding job is understanding unfamiliar code. The brief lists these five items as the read-only base of the coding area (doc: knowledge-base/data/area-briefs/067-coding-capabilities-and-developer-workflows.md S67.01 to S67.05). The product matrix records code sessions as present on Web, Desktop, Mobile, CLI and VS Code and absent on the Chrome extension (doc: docs/product/surface-feature-matrix.md:412-419).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers who open a folder in the Desktop app, the CLI or VS Code, and developers who watch or steer a Desktop session from the phone. New team members use it to learn a codebase.
problems_solved: Reading a large unfamiliar repository by hand is slow.
Text search alone does not explain how parts fit together.
A person away from the computer still wants to check what a session found.
use_cases: On Desktop, open a folder and ask where the sign-in check is implemented.
In the CLI, run a one-shot prompt asking for a map of the main parts of the repository.
In VS Code, ask in the sidebar chat who calls a function.
On the phone, open a running Desktop session and read the answer.

where_to_find_it: Desktop (Electron shell): the Code page, chip labelled 'Work with local code', then a folder session panel (apps/web/features/code/code-surface.ts:116; apps/web/features/code/CloudCodePage.tsx:1949).

Web in a plain browser: the /code page offers cloud sessions only; the setup chips are 'Terminal', 'VS Code' and 'Desktop app' (apps/web/features/code/code-surface.ts:112-114). The local folder panel is not reachable without the Desktop shell (apps/web/features/code/hooks/use-local-sessions.ts:121).
CLI: the interactive agi session, or the non-interactive Exec subcommand with alias e (apps/cli/src/lib.rs:767).
VS Code: the AGI sidebar chat; the editor commands 'Code: Explain Selection', 'Code: Explain Terminal Output' and 'Code: Explain Error' (apps/extension-vscode/package.json:137, 335, 345).

Mobile: the screen titled 'AGI Code'; a session opens from the list, composer placeholder 'Message this session' (apps/mobile/src/features/companion/components/codeSessionTimeline.ts:8-13; packages/contracts/types/src/pairing.ts:30).
Chrome extension: not available (doc: docs/product/surface-feature-matrix.md:419).
prerequisites: Desktop: an approved folder and the agent grant for that folder; without it the folder is listed with its sessions withheld (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:985-1000).

A model the session can reach: an on-device model, a provider the person signed in to in the CLI, or the account's cloud models, which need a plan with the developer_surfaces capability (apps/web/features/code/local-code.ts:708).

steps.what_happens: The person types a question in the Desktop session panel and presses Enter.
The desktop shell checks the folder grant for the agent, then relays the turn to the CLI app-server it spawned in that folder.
The agent calls read-only tools on the folder (read, grep, glob, list). These read local files.
The agent sends prompts and tool results to the chosen model. For an on-device model this stays on the device; for the account's cloud models or the person's own provider it leaves the device.
For a cloud model on the account route, the model call goes through our servers under plan checks; the CLI signs in with a developer token the gateway admits only on plans with developer surfaces.
On Mobile, the phone sends the follow-up through the remote-control link to the computer, which runs the turn; the phone shows the replayed transcript.
On Web in a browser, a cloud session reads files inside a managed sandbox, not on the person's computer.

access_and_usage.account: Folder sessions on Desktop: no account is needed to use an on-device model [inferred]; the account route needs sign-in. Whether the CLI app-server requires sign-in before a local model runs was not established. Cloud sandbox: signed-in account required (apps/web/app/api/code/sessions/[sessionId]/changes/route.ts:31 uses getUserScopedDb).
access_and_usage.permissions: Desktop: per-folder grant for the agent (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/agentAccess.ts:23). Reads of a running session need filesystem.read or the agent grant (apps/desktop/electron/runtime/dispatcher.ts:985-1000). CLI: workspace policy can deny or ask for any tool (apps/cli/src/features/exec/tools/mod.rs:592).
access_and_usage.subscription: Cloud models in a folder session need the developer_surfaces capability: plan:pro, plan:max, plan:max_15x, plan:team, plan:team_premium, plan:enterprise (packages/contracts/types/src/billing-catalog.ts:359). The cloud sandbox needs a plan with sandboxes and a code daily budget: plan:basic, plan:pro, plan:max, plan:max_15x, plan:team, plan:team_premium, plan:enterprise; not plan:free, plan:byok or plan:local-only (packages/contracts/types/src/billing-catalog.ts:594, 611, 628, 839).
access_and_usage.limits_and_metering: Phone-started sessions are limited to 10 starts per 10 minutes and 8 running at once (packages/platform/utils/src/remoteControl/codeRemoteController.ts:44-46). Sandbox count and daily code budget come from plan limits (packages/contracts/types/src/billing-catalog.ts:801-841). Metering for folder sessions on the account route is done by the gateway; details not read.
access_and_usage.flags: AGI_E2B_EXECUTION and E2B_API_KEY switch the cloud sandbox on (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts:6-7). The managed-compute private beta gate is separate (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts:34-36).

access_and_usage.local_mode: A folder session with an on-device model works with no paid plan: the plan line is shown only when the draft needs account cloud models, and the notice offers 'Upgrade' and 'Set up a local model' (apps/web/features/code/CloudCodePage.tsx:2120-2146; apps/web/features/code/local-code.ts:824-833). features.summary: The coding agent edits and creates files in the approved folder to do a job: build a feature, fix a defect, refactor, write tests or docs, migrate, upgrade dependencies. Each write or command is checked against folder access and the approval mode first. On a plain Web tab it runs in a cloud sandbox instead.

purpose.what_it_does: Turns a plain request into file changes. The agent reads first, then edits or writes files, and asks the person before risky steps. It covers feature work, defect fixes, refactors, new tests, docs, migrations and dependency upgrades; all seven brief items use the same editing tools.
purpose.why_it_exists: Editing code is the main job of a coding assistant. The brief gives one 'Should' line per task type (doc: knowledge-base/data/area-briefs/067-coding-capabilities-and-developer-workflows.md S67.06-S67.09, S67.26-S67.28).
purpose.who_uses_it: Developers on Desktop, CLI and VS Code; developers who start or steer a Desktop session from the phone; Web users with a plan that includes the cloud sandbox.
problems_solved: Repetitive multi-file edits take long by hand.
Writing tests and docs is skipped for lack of time.
Upgrades need many small code changes.
use_cases: Ask the agent to add a field across a form, its API and its tests.
Paste a failing stack trace and ask for the fix.
Ask for unit tests for an untested module.
Ask to rename a module and update every import.

established.statement: Given a feature request, the agent edits and creates files.
Given a defect, the agent finds the cause and edits the code.
The agent restructures code across files without changing behaviour.
The agent writes new test files or cases.
The agent writes or updates documentation from the code.
The agent performs a code or schema migration across the repository.
The agent upgrades dependencies and adjusts code.
An action a user cannot undo asks first and names the consequence.

acceptance_criteria: Ask for a one-file edit with mode ask; an approval card appears showing the patch before the file changes.
Deny the approval; the file is unchanged and the agent is told it was refused.
With mode plan, no file is written.
Edit a path outside the approved folder; the write is refused.
In a plain browser tab with the sandbox off, no edit is possible and the page says so.
Ask the agent to add tests; new test files exist and appear in the changes panel.

Dependency upgrades and migrations need shell approval because they run package commands. [inferred]
proposed: [proposed] Show a plain-language preview of every write on Web cloud sessions the same way VS Code does.
[proposed] Add a test that runs the whole path signed out with an on-device model.

steps.what_happens: The person sends a request in the composer; the desktop shell checks the folder grant.
The CLI agent plans tool calls and asks the model what to do next.
Before a write the CLI resolves the target against the workspace root and checks workspace policy, then asks for approval unless the mode pre-approves edits.
The approval request is shown in the app and the answer returns to the CLI.

features.summary: The coding agent runs the project's own test, type check, lint and build commands in the folder, after the person approves the command, then reads the output and explains or fixes failures. Desktop also has a test-run helper that detects the test command itself. A non-zero exit is reported, never read as a pass.

purpose.what_it_does: Runs the project's checks inside the approved folder and gives the result and output back to the agent and the person. The agent can then explain the failure or change code to fix it.
purpose.why_it_exists: A change is only trustworthy if the project's own checks pass. The brief requires the agent to run tests, type checks, linters and builds and to interpret failures (doc: knowledge-base/data/area-briefs/067-coding-capabilities-and-developer-workflows.md S67.10-S67.14).
